claim: Meta-analysis of transcriptomic experiments from muscles of ALS patients and mouse models uncovered p53 deregulation as a common denominator.
source: We meta-analyzed transcriptomic experiments of muscles of ALS patients and mouse models, uncovering a p53 deregulation as common denominator.
evidence: The abstract states this finding directly, and it is supported by the bioinformatic analyses described in the Results section using four independent microarray experiments.

claim: Several p53 family members (p53, p63, p73) are induced in muscles during ALS.
source: We then characterized the induction of several p53 family members (p53, p63, p73) and a correlation between the levels of p53 family target genes and the severity of muscle atrophy in ALS patients and mice.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by RT-qPCR and protein expression data shown in Figures 2, 3, and 4.

claim: The levels of p53 family target genes correlate with the severity of muscle atrophy in ALS patients and mice.
source: We then characterized the induction of several p53 family members (p53, p63, p73) and a correlation between the levels of p53 family target genes and the severity of muscle atrophy in ALS patients and mice.
evidence: This correlation is demonstrated in Figure 1B showing correlation between gene expression and muscle injury scores.

claim: Increased p63 protein levels are observed in the fibers of atrophic muscles via denervation-dependent and -independent mechanisms.
source: In particular, we observed increased p63 protein levels in the fibers of atrophic muscles via denervation-dependent and -independent mechanisms.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by nerve crush experiments (Figure 5A-D) and SOD1 overexpression experiments (Figure 5E).

claim: TAp63 and p53 transactivate the promoter of Trim63 (MuRF1).
source: At a functional level, we demonstrated that TAp63 and p53 transactivate the promoter and increased the expression of Trim63 (MuRF1), an effector of muscle atrophy.
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase reporter assays in Figure 7A-B and ChIP experiments in Figure 7C.

claim: TAp63 and p53 increase the expression of Trim63 (MuRF1).
source: At a functional level, we demonstrated that TAp63 and p53 transactivate the promoter and increased the expression of Trim63 (MuRF1), an effector of muscle atrophy.
evidence: This is shown by RT-qPCR data in Figure 6B and siRNA knockdown experiments in Figure 7D.

claim: Trim63 (MuRF1) is an effector of muscle atrophy.
source: At a functional level, we demonstrated that TAp63 and p53 transactivate the promoter and increased the expression of Trim63 (MuRF1), an effector of muscle atrophy.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited in the manuscript regarding the role of E3 ubiquitin ligases in muscle atrophy.

claim: p63 contributes to muscular atrophic processes via the regulation of multiple genes, including the muscle atrophy gene Trim63.
source: Altogether, these results suggest a novel function for p63 as a contributor to muscular atrophic processes via the regulation of multiple genes, including the muscle atrophy gene Trim63.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, supported by the combined data from expression analyses, functional assays, and promoter studies.

claim: Muscle atrophy is associated with aging, cancer, AIDS and neurodegenerative diseases such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).
source: Muscle atrophy is associated with aging, cancer, AIDS and neurodegenerative diseases such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) (von Haehling et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a general statement supported by a citation to von Haehling et al., 2010.

claim: Atrophy and dysfunction of respiratory muscles lead to death in ALS patients.
source: For example, atrophy and dysfunction of respiratory muscles lead to death in ALS patients (Rothstein, 2009).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Rothstein, 2009.

claim: Around 20% of all inherited ALS cases can be linked to mutations in the gene encoding SOD1.
source: Around 20% of all inherited ALS cases can be linked to mutations in the gene encoding SOD1.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in ALS research presented as background knowledge.

claim: ALS-associated SOD1 mutations trigger aggregation of SOD1 proteins in the cytoplasm.
source: Cellular events (Pansarasa et al., 2014) that have been shown to be triggered by these different mutations include aggregation of SOD1 proteins in the cytoplasm (Hart, 2006), increase in oxidative stress (Barber and Shaw, 2010) and subsequent DNA damage (Aguirre et al., 2005), endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress (Nishitoh et al., 2008) or alterations of mitochondrial function (Manfredi and Xu, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hart, 2006.

claim: ALS-associated SOD1 mutations trigger increase in oxidative stress.
source: Cellular events (Pansarasa et al., 2014) that have been shown to be triggered by these different mutations include aggregation of SOD1 proteins in the cytoplasm (Hart, 2006), increase in oxidative stress (Barber and Shaw, 2010) and subsequent DNA damage (Aguirre et al., 2005), endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress (Nishitoh et al., 2008) or alterations of mitochondrial function (Manfredi and Xu, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Barber and Shaw, 2010.

claim: ALS-associated SOD1 mutations trigger DNA damage.
source: Cellular events (Pansarasa et al., 2014) that have been shown to be triggered by these different mutations include aggregation of SOD1 proteins in the cytoplasm (Hart, 2006), increase in oxidative stress (Barber and Shaw, 2010) and subsequent DNA damage (Aguirre et al., 2005), endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress (Nishitoh et al., 2008) or alterations of mitochondrial function (Manfredi and Xu, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Aguirre et al., 2005.

claim: ALS-associated SOD1 mutations trigger endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress.
source: Cellular events (Pansarasa et al., 2014) that have been shown to be triggered by these different mutations include aggregation of SOD1 proteins in the cytoplasm (Hart, 2006), increase in oxidative stress (Barber and Shaw, 2010) and subsequent DNA damage (Aguirre et al., 2005), endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress (Nishitoh et al., 2008) or alterations of mitochondrial function (Manfredi and Xu, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nishitoh et al., 2008.

claim: ALS-associated SOD1 mutations trigger alterations of mitochondrial function.
source: Cellular events (Pansarasa et al., 2014) that have been shown to be triggered by these different mutations include aggregation of SOD1 proteins in the cytoplasm (Hart, 2006), increase in oxidative stress (Barber and Shaw, 2010) and subsequent DNA damage (Aguirre et al., 2005), endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress (Nishitoh et al., 2008) or alterations of mitochondrial function (Manfredi and Xu, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Manfredi and Xu, 2005.

claim: The p53 family members (p53, p63, p73) play an important role in muscle physiopathology.
source: Several observations indicate that the p53 family members (p53, p63, p73) play an important role in muscle physiopathology and might therefore represent actors of the muscle atrophy (Schwarzkopf et al., 2006; Mazzaro et al., 1999; Cam et al., 2006; Fontemaggi et al., 2001; Martin et al., 2011; Rouleau et al., 2011; Belloni et al., 2006; Su et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The p53 family of transcription factors is a central regulator of cellular processes such as apoptosis, cell cycle arrest, metabolism or cellular differentiation.
source: The p53 family of transcription factors is a central regulator of cellular processes such as apoptosis, cell cycle arrest, metabolism or cellular differentiation through the regulation of several target genes (CDKN1A, BAX, GADD45A, MDM2 and others) (Arrowsmith, 1999; Menendez et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Arrowsmith, 1999 and Menendez et al., 2009.

claim: ΔN isoforms lack a canonical transactivation domain and can serve as dominant negatives versus the TA isoforms in some cases.
source: ∆N isoforms lack such a domain and can serve as dominant negatives versus the TA isoforms in some cases, although they are also capable of transactivating certain genes (De Laurenzi et al., 1998; Casciano et al., 1999; Murray-Zmijewski et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to De Laurenzi et al., 1998; Casciano et al., 1999; Murray-Zmijewski et al., 2006.

claim: ΔN isoforms are capable of transactivating certain genes.
source: ∆N isoforms lack such a domain and can serve as dominant negatives versus the TA isoforms in some cases, although they are also capable of transactivating certain genes (De Laurenzi et al., 1998; Casciano et al., 1999; Murray-Zmijewski et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to De Laurenzi et al., 1998; Casciano et al., 1999; Murray-Zmijewski et al., 2006.

claim: p53 is activated during myogenic differentiation.
source: In muscles, p53 is activated during myogenic differentiation, participates with MyoD to induce myogenesis, and mediates doxorubicin-induced muscle atrophy via its target gene pw1 (Schwarzkopf et al., 2006; Mazzaro et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schwarzkopf et al., 2006 and Mazzaro et al., 1999.

claim: p53 participates with MyoD to induce myogenesis.
source: In muscles, p53 is activated during myogenic differentiation, participates with MyoD to induce myogenesis, and mediates doxorubicin-induced muscle atrophy via its target gene pw1 (Schwarzkopf et al., 2006; Mazzaro et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schwarzkopf et al., 2006 and Mazzaro et al., 1999.

claim: p53 mediates doxorubicin-induced muscle atrophy via its target gene pw1.
source: In muscles, p53 is activated during myogenic differentiation, participates with MyoD to induce myogenesis, and mediates doxorubicin-induced muscle atrophy via its target gene pw1 (Schwarzkopf et al., 2006; Mazzaro et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schwarzkopf et al., 2006 and Mazzaro et al., 1999.

claim: p53 expression is not essential for muscle development.
source: Nonetheless, p53 expression is not essential for muscle development (Donehower et al., 1992) or regeneration (White et al., 2002), which could be explained by compensatory mechanisms involving p63 and p73.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Donehower et al., 1992.

claim: p53 expression is not essential for muscle regeneration.
source: Nonetheless, p53 expression is not essential for muscle development (Donehower et al., 1992) or regeneration (White et al., 2002), which could be explained by compensatory mechanisms involving p63 and p73.
evidence: This is supported by citation to White et al., 2002.

claim: p63 and p73 are involved in myoblast differentiation.
source: Indeed, more recent studies have shown that p63 and p73 are also involved in myoblast differentiation (Cam et al., 2006; Fontemaggi et al., 2001; Martin et al., 2011; Rouleau et al., 2011) and ΔNp73 appears to protect muscle cells against stresses (Belloni et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cam et al., 2006; Fontemaggi et al., 2001; Martin et al., 2011; Rouleau et al., 2011.

claim: ΔNp73 appears to protect muscle cells against stresses.
source: Indeed, more recent studies have shown that p63 and p73 are also involved in myoblast differentiation (Cam et al., 2006; Fontemaggi et al., 2001; Martin et al., 2011; Rouleau et al., 2011) and ΔNp73 appears to protect muscle cells against stresses (Belloni et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Belloni et al., 2006.

claim: p63 is important for the regulation of muscle cell metabolism via the regulation of Sirtuins and AMPK.
source: Finally, a study showed that p63 is important for the regulation of muscle cell metabolism via the regulation of Sirtuins and AMPK (Su et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Su et al., 2012.

claim: The activity of p53 was identified to be commonly deregulated in all four microarray experiments that included biopsies from patients and animal models.
source: Interestingly, the activity of only three transcription factors, MyoD, Myogenin and p53, was identified to be commonly deregulated in all four experiments that included biopsies from patients and animal models.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: P53 was the transcription factor with the highest number of deregulated genes (51 genes).
source: P53 was the transcription factor with the highest number of deregulated genes (51 genes).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The p53 target genes CDKN1A, GADD45A and PMAIP1 were found induced in all four experiments.
source: Notably the p53 target genes CDKN1A, GADD45A and PMAIP1, among others, were found induced in all four experiments.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the microarray data analysis.

claim: CDKN1A expression correlated with the degree of the pathology of the muscle from ALS patients.
source: We found that CDKNA1, GADD45A and PMAIP1 expression correlated with the degree of the pathology of the muscle from ALS patients (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1B with correlation coefficients and p-values.

claim: GADD45A expression correlated with the degree of the pathology of the muscle from ALS patients.
source: We found that CDKNA1, GADD45A and PMAIP1 expression correlated with the degree of the pathology of the muscle from ALS patients (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1B with correlation coefficients and p-values.

claim: PMAIP1 expression correlated with the degree of the pathology of the muscle from ALS patients.
source: We found that CDKNA1, GADD45A and PMAIP1 expression correlated with the degree of the pathology of the muscle from ALS patients (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1B with correlation coefficients and p-values.

claim: The expression of P63 correlated with the severity of the pathology in muscles biopsies from ALS patients.
source: In particular, the expression of P63 correlated with the severity of the pathology in muscles biopsies from ALS patients (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: CDKN1A, GADD45A and PMAIP1 were induced in the muscle biopsies of ALS patients.
source: We confirmed that CDKN1A, GADD45A and PMAIP1 were induced in the muscle biopsies of ALS patients (Figure 2A,B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2A-C by RT-qPCR data.

claim: Upregulation of the p53 target genes Gadd45a, Cdkn1a, Bax, Pmaip1 and Perp was observed at 90 days and further increased at 105 days in SOD1(G86R) mice.
source: Upregulation of the p53 target genes Gadd45a, Cdkn1a, Bax, Pmaip1 and Perp was observed at 90 days and further increased at 105 days in SOD1(G86R) mice (Figure 2D,E,F, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2D-F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The mRNA levels of TA isoforms of Trp63 were strongly induced towards the end of the disease (105 day) in SOD1(G86R) mice.
source: Strikingly, the mRNA levels of TA isoforms of Trp63 were strongly induced towards the end of the disease (105 day), while the mRNA levels for ΔN isoforms of Trp63 were downregulated during the same time period.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3.

claim: The mRNA levels for ΔN isoforms of Trp63 were downregulated towards the end of the disease in SOD1(G86R) mice.
source: Strikingly, the mRNA levels of TA isoforms of Trp63 were strongly induced towards the end of the disease (105 day), while the mRNA levels for ΔN isoforms of Trp63 were downregulated during the same time period.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3.

claim: The expression of TA isoforms of Trp63 correlated with acetylcholine receptor alpha (Chrna1) expression in SOD1(G86R) mice.
source: The expression of TA isoforms of Trp63 correlated with acetylcholine receptor alpha (Chrna1) expression, a molecular marker indicating the severity of muscular denervation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3.

claim: The deregulation of Trp63 expression correlated with the upregulation of Fbxo32 (Atrogin-1) and Trim63 (MuRF1) in SOD1(G86R) mice.
source: Importantly, the deregulation of Trp63 expression also correlated with the upregulation of these two markers.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section referring to Fbxo32 and Trim63, and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Immunoblotting with a TAp63 isoforms specific antibody revealed a striking accumulation of p63 proteins in muscles of SOD1 (G86R) mice that correlated with the progression of the disease.
source: Immunoblotting with a TAp63 isoforms specific antibody revealed a striking accumulation of p63 proteins in muscles of SOD1 (G86R) mice that correlated with the progression of the disease (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A by Western blot.

claim: Immunohistochemistry revealed markedly increased immunoreactivity of p63 in the nuclei of muscle fibers of SOD1(G86R) mice.
source: Immunohistochemistry with the same antibody also revealed markedly increased immunoreactivity in the nuclei of muscle fibers of SOD1(G86R) (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Denervation upregulated TAp63 mRNA levels five- to sixfold in wild-type mice.
source: Our results showed that denervation upregulated TAp63 mRNA levels five- to sixfold in wild-type mice (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Denervation downregulated ΔNp63 levels 0.4-fold in wild-type mice.
source: Concomitantly, ΔNp63 levels were downregulated 0.4-fold (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In SOD1(G86R) mice, nerve crush further accentuated changes in mRNA levels for TA and ∆N isoforms of Trp63.
source: In SOD1(G86R) mice, nerve crush further accentuated changes in mRNA levels for TA and ∆N isoforms of Trp63.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: The TAp63 target genes Cdkn1a and Gadd45a were found strongly induced after nerve crush.
source: In addition, the TAp63 target genes Cdkn1a and Gadd45a were found strongly induced after nerve crush (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: Nerve injury leading to alteration of the motor axis is sufficient to activate a TAp63 response.
source: These results show that nerve injury leading to alteration of the motor axis seems to be sufficient to activate a TAp63 response.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the nerve crush experiments shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: Several target genes of the p53-family (Bax, Cdkn1a, Gadd45a) were induced upon overexpression of SOD1(G86R) in C2C12 myoblasts.
source: Several target genes of the p53-family (Bax, Cdkn1a, Gadd45a) were induced upon overexpression of SOD1(G86R) (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5E.

claim: TAp63 expression was increased at the mRNA level and the protein level upon overexpression of SOD1(G86R) in C2C12 myoblasts.
source: Similarly TAp63 expression was increased at the mRNA level and the protein level (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The mRNA levels as well as the promoter activity of △N isoforms of P63 were downregulated upon overexpression of SOD1(G86R) in C2C12 myoblasts.
source: In contrast, the mRNA levels as well as the promoter activity of △N isoforms of P63 were downregulated (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1) (Romano et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: TAp63 represses the promoter activity of the △N isoforms of P63.
source: We observed that TAp63 represses the promoter activity of the △N isoforms of P63, while it expectedly induces the Mdm2 promoter (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Expression of SOD1(G86R) was sufficient to trigger a p53-like response similar to in vivo observations in atrophic muscle tissues.
source: These results demonstrated that expression of SOD1(G86R) was sufficient to trigger a p53-like response similar to our in vivo observations in atrophic muscle tissues.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the C2C12 overexpression experiments shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: TAp63 protein levels increased upon treatment with menadione (oxidative stress), etoposide (DNA damage), FCCP (mitochondrial deregulation), and tunicamycin (ER stress) in C2C12 cells.
source: Treated cells revealed an increase of TAp63 upon the four stresses (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Overexpression of ATF4 induces the RNA level for TAp63.
source: Interestingly, overexpression of ATF4 and ATF6 induces the RNA level for TAp63 and TAp73 respectively, but not p53 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Overexpression of ATF6 induces the RNA level for TAp73.
source: Interestingly, overexpression of ATF4 and ATF6 induces the RNA level for TAp63 and TAp73 respectively, but not p53 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Overexpression of ATF4 and ATF6 does not induce p53 RNA levels.
source: Interestingly, overexpression of ATF4 and ATF6 induces the RNA level for TAp63 and TAp73 respectively, but not p53 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Upregulation of TAp63 expression might be involved in the muscle cell response to diverse stresses including stresses related to SOD1 mutants.
source: This result indicated that upregulation of TAp63 expression might be involved in the muscle cell response to diverse stresses including stresses related to SOD1 mutants.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the stress treatment experiments shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: TAp63 overexpression in C2C12 cells strongly induced Trim63 mRNA levels.
source: Indeed, TAp63 overexpression in C2C12 cells strongly induced Trim63 mRNA levels (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: p53 or p73 had less effect on Trim63 expression compared to TAp63 in C2C12 cells.
source: Note that under this condition p53 or p73 had less effect on Trim63 expression (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: p53 family members induced Trim63 promoter reporters that contained at least the fragment -500 bp to -1000 bp.
source: We found that p53 family members induced Trim63 promoter reporters that contained at least the fragment -500 bp to -1000 bp (Figure 7A and B) (Waddell et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7A-B.

claim: TAp63 proteins bound preferentially onto RE1/2 binding sites in the Trim63 promoter.
source: Chromatin immunoprecipitation experiments (ChIP) covering RE1/2 and RE4 binding sites showed that TAp63 proteins bound preferentially onto RE1/2 (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7C by ChIP experiments.

claim: p73 and p53 bound to RE1/2 binding sites in the Trim63 promoter.
source: Similarly, ChIP experiments indicated that p73 and p53 bound to RE1/2 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: p73 also bound to RE4 binding sites in the Trim63 promoter.
source: However, p73 seemed also to bind RE4.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section referring to ChIP data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Silencing of TAp63 reduced Trim63 mRNA levels in both basal state and following stress induced by FCCP in C2C12 cells.
source: Importantly, silencing of TAp63 reduced Trim63 mRNA levels in both basal state and following stress induced by FCCP (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7D.

claim: SiRNA against p53 diminished Trim63 RNA level in C2C12 cells.
source: SiRNA against p53 also diminished Trim63 RNA level, while siRNA against p73 had not significant effect (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: SiRNA against p73 had no significant effect on Trim63 RNA level in C2C12 cells.
source: SiRNA against p53 also diminished Trim63 RNA level, while siRNA against p73 had not significant effect (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The combination of siRNA against TA isoforms of Trp63, TA isoforms of P73 and P53 diminished Trim63 RNA level up to ~50%, but did not abolish it.
source: The combination of siRNA against TA isoforms of Trp63, TA isoforms of P73 and P53 diminished further Trim63 RNA level up to ~50%, but did not abolish it.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section referring to data in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The direct binding of p63 and p53 to the Trim63 promoter correlates with the modification of gene expression in C2C12 muscular cells.
source: Taken together, these results indicate a complex regulation of the Trim63 promoter, in which the direct binding of p63 and p53 correlates with the modification of gene expression in C2C12 muscular cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined ChIP and expression data shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: The deregulation of p63 and p63 target genes occurs in muscle of ALS patients that have not been selected for a particular genetic alteration.
source: Our observation that the deregulation of p63 and p63 target genes occurs in muscle of ALS patients that have not been selected for a particular genetic alteration indicates that these deregulations are likely to be a common feature in ALS, independently of whether it is SOD1 that is mutated or another gene.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the patient data.

claim: p63 participates in muscle cell differentiation and metabolism.
source: It was previously reported that p63 participates in muscle cell differentiation and metabolism, and contributes to cardiac muscle development (Cam et al., 2006; Martin et al., 2011; Rouleau et al., 2011; Su et al., 2012; Osada et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to previous studies.

claim: p63 contributes to cardiac muscle development.
source: It was previously reported that p63 participates in muscle cell differentiation and metabolism, and contributes to cardiac muscle development (Cam et al., 2006; Martin et al., 2011; Rouleau et al., 2011; Su et al., 2012; Osada et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to previous studies.

claim: Genetic inactivation of p53 does not affect ALS progression.
source: However, genetic inactivation of p53 does not affect ALS progression, muscle development or muscle regenerative capacity (Donehower et al., 1992; White et al., 2002; Kuntz et al., 2000; Prudlo et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to previous studies.

claim: Genetic inactivation of p53 does not affect muscle development.
source: However, genetic inactivation of p53 does not affect ALS progression, muscle development or muscle regenerative capacity (Donehower et al., 1992; White et al., 2002; Kuntz et al., 2000; Prudlo et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to previous studies.

claim: Genetic inactivation of p53 does not affect muscle regenerative capacity.
source: However, genetic inactivation of p53 does not affect ALS progression, muscle development or muscle regenerative capacity (Donehower et al., 1992; White et al., 2002; Kuntz et al., 2000; Prudlo et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to previous studies.

claim: The absence of p53 could be compensated by p63 or p73.
source: Nevertheless, our results suggest that the absence of p53 could be compensated by p63 or even p73.
evidence: This is a speculation stated in the Discussion section based on the observed expression patterns.

claim: P63 deregulation can have an intercellular origin represented by the loss of interaction between the muscle and the nerve cells.
source: For instance, we showed that P63 deregulation could have an intercellular origin represented by the loss of interaction between the muscle and the nerve cells, as provoked in the nerve crush experiment (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section referring to the nerve crush experiments in Figure 5.

claim: P63 deregulation can have an intrinsic origin resulting from expression of SOD1(G86R) in muscle cells causing intracellular stresses.
source: However, we also observed that P63 deregulation can have an intrinsic origin resulting from expression of SOD1(G86R) in muscle cells causing intracellular stresses (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section referring to the C2C12 overexpression experiments in Figure 5.

claim: ALS-associated SOD1 mutations induce SOD1 protein aggregates in muscle cells.
source: Indeed, ALS-associated SOD1 mutations have been shown to induce SOD1 protein aggregates and mitochondrial dysfunction in muscle cells (Pansarasa et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Pansarasa et al., 2014.

claim: ALS-associated SOD1 mutations induce mitochondrial dysfunction in muscle cells.
source: Indeed, ALS-associated SOD1 mutations have been shown to induce SOD1 protein aggregates and mitochondrial dysfunction in muscle cells (Pansarasa et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Pansarasa et al., 2014.

claim: Both activation of a protein aggregate stress response pathway and mitochondrial dysfunction could induce a TAp63 response.
source: Interestingly, we observed that both activation of a protein aggregate stress response pathway or mitochondrial dysfunction could induce a TAp63 response.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section referring to the stress treatment experiments in Figure 5F.

claim: tp63 is an effector of the ER stress pathway in zebrafish allowing the regulation of the pro-apoptotic gene bbc3 (puma).
source: This finding is supported by a previous report showing that tp63 is an effector of the ER stress pathway in zebrafish allowing the regulation of the pro-apoptotic gene bbc3 (puma) (Pyati et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Pyati et al., 2011.

claim: ATF4 and ATF6 were able to induce the RNA levels of TA isoforms of Trp63 and P73 in C2C12 cells.
source: We showed that some of these transcription factors, notably ATF4 and ATF6, were able to induce the RNA levels of TA isoforms of Trp63 and P73 in C2C12 cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section referring to data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The majority of the p53/p63/p73 target genes upregulated during ALS in the atrophic muscles are connected to cell death.
source: Our study revealed that the majority of the p53/p63/p73 target genes upregulated during ALS in the atrophic muscles are connected to cell death (Gadd45a, Peg3, Perp, Pmaip1, Bax, Siva, Eda2r, Wig1/Pag608) (Figure 1 and Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section referring to data in Figure 1 and Table 1.

claim: Overexpression of TAp63 induces cell death in C2C12 myoblasts.
source: Second, overexpression of TAp63 induces cell death in C2C12 myoblasts (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section referring to data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 (likely Figure 7—figure supplement 2 based on the figures provided).

claim: The expression of Trim63 involves several transcription factors, such as FOXO1 and the glucocorticoid receptors.
source: The first is that the expression of Trim63 involves several transcription factors, such as FOXO1 and the glucocorticoid receptors that certainly participate in the regulation of Trim63 during ALS.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an explanation for incomplete knockdown effects.

claim: The coordinated silencing of p53, TAp63 and TAp73 did not completely abolish Trim63 RNA levels.
